strengths: The paper addresses an important, underexplored NLP/speech problem and makes a coherent case that transcript-centric chaptering and evaluation omit relevant acoustic and temporal information.

The comparison spans text models, hand-crafted acoustic augmentation, an audio-only architecture, and multimodal LLMs. The consistent advantage of Whisper-based AudioSeg over the evaluated text systems is substantial, while the duration- and speaker-stratified analyses expose meaningful limitations rather than relying only on aggregate scores.

The formal distinction among reference-text, ASR-text, discrete-time, and continuous-time evaluation is clear and useful. The oracle analysis, granularity checks, and continuous-time collar evaluation provide good evidence that transcript choice and sentence discretization can distort comparisons.

Ablations identify pauses as the principal useful hand-crafted cue and provide some evidence for non-speech information through speech-enhancement filtering. The extensive appendices include prompts, feature extraction procedures, hyperparameters, failure analyses, and multiple evaluation variants.
The work is relevant to ACL and appears sufficiently sound for Findings; its combination of methodology, modeling, and empirical analysis also creates a credible case for main-conference publication.
weaknesses: The paper repeatedly interprets AudioSeg's advantage as evidence that audio captures information beyond transcripts, but the strongest encoder is Whisper Large, an ASR-pretrained model that encodes substantial linguistic content. The comparison establishes transcript-free inference, not that acoustic information itself explains the gain. Controlled experiments using matched-capacity semantic and acoustic representations, shuffled or masked speech content, or text-audio fusion are needed for the stronger mechanistic claim.

The empirical superiority claim is broader than the baseline evidence supports. The main supervised text comparator is MiniSeg, while stronger recent long-context chaptering or segmentation systems are discussed but not evaluated. AudioSeg also uses a much larger pretrained backbone, so the experiments do not isolate modality from model capacity, pretraining data, or possible YouTube-domain overlap.

Statistical reliability is insufficiently documented: results appear to come from single runs, with no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance across seeds. This is especially problematic for small differences in the feature and protocol analyses, and for AMI, whose reported test sets contain only 16 meetings overall and just four under 30 minutes.

The claimed cross-domain validation is weak. The AMI experiment is very small, its annotation and adaptation procedure is underspecified, and the YTSeg-to-AMI models appear to be further trained on AMI rather than evaluated zero-shot. It therefore demonstrates transfer initialization more than broad domain generalization.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive appendix. The manuscript does not clearly state the YTSeg split sizes and construction, random seeds, decision thresholds and model-selection procedure, AudioSeg compute requirements, or several preprocessing and truncation details. The asserted public release is not concretely accessible from the manuscript.

The proposed title evaluation is only a limited diagnostic: temporal matching excludes unmatched chapters and thus can report high title similarity on a very small matched subset, while global concatenation conflates title content, ordering, and chapter count. These measures do not strongly substantiate title-quality claims.

The main findings are much weaker for long recordings—the motivating setting—with severe degradation beyond 30 minutes and very low performance at 60 minutes or more. MLLM results are also largely restricted to recordings below 30 minutes. This limitation should constrain the paper's broad framing of long-form audio chaptering.
